name: Eazovir
description: Eazovir is a synthetic opioid-receptor partial agonist combined with autonomic nervous system stabilizers, specifically engineered to suppress the physical symptoms of acute withdrawal — vomiting, muscle cramping, hyperhidrosis, tachycardia, insomnia — without providing the euphoric reward signal that perpetuates dependency cycles. Helix markets it as 'withdrawal without the war,' and it largely delivers on that promise for opioid, synthetic opioid, and certain stimulant withdrawal presentations. It is itself mildly habit-forming with extended use, a fact Helix's marketing materials treat with notable understatement.
effects: Rapid suppression of nausea, vomiting, and gastrointestinal withdrawal symptoms
Relief from muscle cramping, restless limb syndrome, and hyperhidrosis
Cardiovascular stabilization — normalizes elevated heart rate and blood pressure
Mild sedative effect enabling sleep during acute withdrawal
Reduction of anxiety and agitation without full anxiolytic blunting
side_effects: Mild physical dependency develops after 3+ weeks of daily use
Requires its own gradual taper to discontinue safely
Mild cognitive fogging in first few days
Users who exceed recommended dose experience a low-grade euphoria — the primary vector for Eazovir misuse
Rare: respiratory depression in users with compromised pulmonary systems or when combined with depressants
street_price: Φ55 per tab (Φ180 per week supply)
cultural_context: Eazovir occupies an uncomfortable middle ground in GLMZ's recovery culture — genuinely helpful, widely available, and quietly predatory. Helix positions it as a humane solution to withdrawal suffering, and for short-term use it is. But the Shelf is full of people who got off their primary substance only to find themselves Eazovir-dependent eighteen months later. Nightshade Pharmatech distributes a superdosed version called 'Ease+' that strips out the autonomic stabilizers and doubles the partial agonist load — it's basically a weak opioid in recovery packaging.
story_hooks: A Shelf medic has been handing out Eazovir to anyone coming off hard opioids — genuinely trying to help — but their supply came from Nightshade and something in this batch is different

A Helix Biosystems internal document has leaked suggesting the company deliberately calibrated Eazovir's dependency threshold to maximize repeat prescription cycles — someone needs that document buried, and someone else needs it very much in the open
A character is managing a dangerous informant through withdrawal using Eazovir as both medicine and leverage — but the informant is smarter about what's happening than they're letting on
